title: Turn the hearts (Malachi 4:5–6)
hookLine: the last lines of the Protestant Old Testament: hearts of parents turned to children

lines: THE FINAL WORD IS ABOUT FAMILIES.
cards: In a Protestant Bible, the Old Testament ends with Malachi. Turn the page, and the next thing is the first line of Matthew, a list of names. Between them sits a silence the Bible doesn't fill.
So whatever Malachi says last stands right at the seam. You might expect a grand vision, or a thunderclap. Instead, the final words are about something small and close to home.
Families. Parents and children. Who's speaking to whom, and who isn't.

teach.b: Malachi's name means my messenger, and it may be a title rather than a name. His book is a series of arguments between God and the people, about tired worship, broken promises and marriages, and the poor being cheated.

Then the end, in the King James Bible: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD: And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers."

teach.h: ELIJAH, CARRIED UP IN A WHIRLWIND.
teach.b: Elijah doesn't die in 2 Kings; he's carried up in a whirlwind. So the hope grew that he'd come back, to prepare the way for God. At the Passover seder, Jewish tradition pours a cup for Elijah and opens the door for him.

And look at Elijah's work: not defeating enemies, but mending families, turning hearts across the generations, both ways. Then the very last words warn that otherwise God will strike the land with a curse.
That ending is so hard that in synagogue readings the verse before it is read again afterward, so the book closes on Elijah and hope. These words come back soon.
In the opening chapter of Luke, an angel promises that a child named John will come in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children.

teach.h: HE SHALL TURN THE HEART OF THE FATHERS.
teach.b: Christians read John the Baptist as the Elijah Malachi promised. So the Old Testament, in this arrangement, ends with a family reunion still waiting to happen.

how: Some churches read Malachi in Advent, as the prophecy of a messenger before the Lord, and pair it with the Gospel stories of John the Baptist.

o: my king, a royal name for a ruler of Judah
my messenger, maybe a title more than a name
my redeemer, a name given to Elijah

games.q: what's inside Malachi 4 — tap the pairs.

s: every Bible ends the Old Testament with Malachi
Protestant Bibles do. the Jewish Bible ends with Chronicles, and other Bibles order the books differently.
Malachi promises Elijah will turn hearts in both directions
parents toward children, and children toward parents.
Jewish tradition sets a cup for Elijah at the Passover seder
a cup is poured for him, and the door is opened during the meal.

games.q: Elijah is coming back before the great day of the LORD. what does Malachi say his work will be?
o: turning the hearts of parents and children toward each other.
games.why: not battles but families: "he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers."

practice: Bring to mind someone a generation away from you, a parent or a child, or if they're gone or far away, a grandparent, a niece, a mentor, and notice what's between you: warmth, distance, an old hurt, a thing unsaid.
Don't try to fix it all; just let your heart turn toward them a few degrees, the way Malachi pictures it. If you pray, bring them before God by name; if not, simply hold them in mind with care.

wordCard.voice: Malachi, meaning my messenger: his last promise that Elijah would come and turn the hearts of parents to children, and children to parents.

orig.note: Hebrew: my messenger. it may be a title for the prophet rather than his name.

carryVoice: Your line: open the door for Elijah. Hearts turn both ways, parents and children alike. Until tomorrow.
